author: Sunluss
quote: Jason Might Be the Worst Protagonist Rockstar Has Ever Written. While I appreciate the pacing of GTA 6, I find its story increasingly frustrating, largely because of how poorly Jason is characterised. He comes across as painfully bland, spineless and lacking any real personality or conviction. My biggest issue is the disconnect between Jason’s decisions and the choices I would personally make. I understand that this is a narrative-driven game and that I’m playing an established character rather than creating my own. I don’t expect complete freedom over every decision, but I do expect a protagonist whose actions I can at least understand, respect or find compelling. There’s something uniquely frustrating about having to actively participate in choices you find humiliating. It’s one thing to watch a fictional character behave in a way you disagree with; it’s another to spend hours personally carrying out those actions. Rather than feeling like a capable, independent protagonist, I feel like some spineless chore boy, constantly doing other people’s bidding without meaningful resistance. Jason doesn’t make me feel powerful, respected or invested in his circumstances. He makes me feel like a glorified errand boy with absolutely no backbone. This is particularly disappointing coming from Rockstar, a studio responsible for characters like Arthur Morgan, John Marston and Niko Bellic. These characters made plenty of questionable decisions, but they possessed distinct personalities, principles and motivations. Even when I disagreed with their actions, I could understand why they made those choices. With Jason, I struggle to find that same justification. His decisions feel less like those of an independently minded individual and more like the behaviour of someone who simply allows himself to be pushed around. I don’t need Jason to reflect my personality or morality. I simply need him to be someone whose decisions feel justified by compelling motivations. A protagonist can be weak, submissive or easily manipulated and still be brilliantly written. But Jason’s apparent passivity doesn’t make him interesting; it makes him insufferable. Ultimately, I enjoy the pacing and graphics, but the more the story progresses, the more I resent being forced to play as a character whose choices I find fundamentally objectionable. For a studio responsible for some of gaming’s greatest protagonists, Jason feels like an extraordinary step backwards.
